column1: The presence of {{c1::Ca2+ (calcium)::ion}} ions in saliva is essential for the biological function of {{c2::protecting teeth::purpose}} [cite: 161].
column2: Calcium helps in the remineralization of tooth enamel.

column1: The salivary enzyme {{c1::amylase::name}} (also known as {{c2::ptyalin::alias}}) is responsible for the initial digestion of {{c3::starch::substrate}} [cite: 162].
column2: Amylase breaks down complex carbohydrates into simpler sugars like maltose.

column1: Saliva contains {{c1::mucin::substance}}, a type of {{c2::glycoprotein::molecule type}} that functions to {{c3::lubricate food::purpose}} for easier swallowing [cite: 163].
column2: Mucin gives saliva its viscous, slippery texture.

column1: Besides water and enzymes, saliva contains {{c1::immunoglobulins::immune component}} for immune defense and allows for the absorption of {{c2::nitrates::substance}} [cite: 164, 165].
column2: The oral mucosa can be a site for rapid absorption of certain chemicals.

column1: The neurological pathway for saliva secretion involves the {{c1::salivatory nucleus::specific brain region}} in the {{c2::medulla::brainstem part}}, which communicates with glands via {{c3::parasympathetic::division of ANS}} nerves [cite: 167].
column2: Activation of the parasympathetic system results in 'watery' saliva rich in enzymes.

column1: {{c1::Atropine::drug}} is a {{c2::muscarinic inhibitor::mechanism}} used clinically as a treatment for excessive {{c3::drooling::symptom}} [cite: 168].
column2: By blocking muscarinic receptors, it inhibits the parasympathetic stimulus for salivation.

column1: {{c1::Xerostomia::term}} is the clinical term for dry mouth, and it can be diagnosed using the {{c2::dry cracker::test name}} test [cite: 169, 170].
column2: In this test, a patient is asked to eat a dry cracker; those with xerostomia will struggle to swallow it without water.

column1: The process of swallowing (deglutition) is divided into {{c1::3::number}} distinct phases: {{c2::buccal}}, {{c3::pharyngeal}}, and {{c4::oesophageal}} [cite: 171, 172].
column2:
These phases transition from voluntary control to involuntary reflex.
[Image of the 3 phases of swallowing]

column1: The {{c1::buccal::phase name}} phase of swallowing is {{c2::voluntary::control type}} and is controlled by the {{c3::cerebral cortex::brain region}} [cite: 173].
column2: This is the only phase under conscious control.

column1: During the buccal phase, the {{c1::tongue contracts::action}} to move food to the top of the {{c2::pharynx::location}}, which activates {{c3::mechanoreceptors::receptor type}} [cite: 174, 175].
column2: This activation triggers the involuntary reflex stages.

column1: The swallowing center is located in the {{c1::medulla::brain region}}, and the primary efferent nerve involved in the reflex is the {{c2::vagus::nerve}} nerve [cite: 175].
column2: The vagus nerve (CN X) coordinates the complex muscle movements of the throat.

column1: During the {{c1::pharyngeal::phase name}} phase of swallowing, the {{c2::uvula::structure}} rises to close the nasal passage, and the {{c3::epiglottis::structure}} closes the trachea [cite: 176, 177].
column2: This prevents food from entering the respiratory tract (aspiration).

column1: During the involuntary pharyngeal phase, respiration is inhibited for approximately {{c1::1 second::duration}} [cite: 178].
column2: This 'swallowing apnea' is a protective mechanism for the lungs.

column1: The {{c1::oesophageal::phase name}} phase of swallowing is {{c2::involuntary::control type}} and relies on {{c3::peristalsis::mechanism}} to move food [cite: 179, 180].
column2: Peristalsis is a wave-like contraction of smooth muscle.

column1: The transit time for swallowing {{c1::fluids::substance}} is 1-2 seconds, whereas {{c2::solids::substance}} take approximately {{c3::4-8::duration}} seconds [cite: 181, 182].
column2: Gravity helps fluids, while solids rely more heavily on peristaltic waves.

column1: Difficulty in swallowing is clinically known as {{c1::dysphagia::term}}, which is common in patients who have suffered a {{c2::stroke::event}} or have {{c3::Parkinson's::disease}} disease [cite: 183, 184].
column2: Dysphagia can lead to malnutrition or aspiration pneumonia.

column1: Neuromuscular issues or {{c1::outpouchings::structural issue}} in the pharynx/oesophagus can lead to swallowing disorders [cite: 185, 186].
column2: Structural abnormalities can trap food or impede its passage.

column1: {{c1::Achalasia::condition}} is a condition where the {{c2::lower oesophageal sphincter::structure}} fails to open properly, often caused by damage to the {{c3::myenteric plexus::nervous structure}} [cite: 187, 188].
column2: The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus is responsible for coordinating GI tract motility.

column1: In the stomach, food is mixed with acid to create {{c1::chyme::substance}}, which is then propelled into the {{c2::duodenum::location}} [cite: 189, 191].
column2: The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine.

column1: {{c1::Pepsin::enzyme}} is the primary enzyme for {{c2::protein::substrate}} digestion in the stomach, while {{c3::intrinsic factor::substance}} is essential for the absorption of {{c4::Vitamin B12::nutrient}} [cite: 192, 193].
column2: Vitamin B12 is vital for red blood cell production; a deficiency can lead to pernicious anemia.

column1: Gastric glands contain {{c1::4::number}} main types of secretory cells: mucus cells, {{c2::parietal::cell type}} cells, {{c3::chief::cell type}} cells, and {{c4::enteroendocrine::cell type}} cells [cite: 194].
column2:
Each cell type has a specific role in maintaining the gastric environment.
[Image of stomach gastric glands showing mucus, parietal, and chief cells]

column1: {{c1::Parietal::cell type}} cells in the stomach are responsible for secreting {{c2::HCl (hydrochloric acid)::substance}} and {{c3::intrinsic factor::substance}} [cite: 196].
column2: These cells are the target of many acid-reducing medications.

column1: {{c1::Chief::cell type}} cells secrete the inactive proenzyme {{c2::pepsinogen::substance}}, which is converted into active {{c3::pepsin::substance}} at a pH of {{c4::2::pH value}} [cite: 197].
column2: The acidic environment is necessary for this proteolytic activation.

column1: Enteroendocrine {{c1::ECL::cell type}} cells secrete {{c2::histamine::hormone/paracrine}}, while {{c3::G cells::cell type}} secrete {{c4::gastrin::hormone}}; both substances {{c5::increase::effect on acid}} acid secretion [cite: 198, 199, 200].
column2: These are paracrine and endocrine regulators of stomach acidity.

column1: The three main purposes of the stomach's acidic conditions are to activate {{c1::pepsin::enzyme}}, kill {{c2::bacteria::microbe type}}, and break down {{c3::cellulose::substance}} [cite: 201, 202, 203, 204].
column2: Stomach acid provides a chemical barrier against pathogens.

column1: In parietal cells, the reaction {{c1::CO2 + H2O::reactants}} = {{c2::H2CO3::intermediate}} → {{c3::H+ and HCO3-::products}} provides the ions for acid secretion [cite: 206].
column2:
The enzyme carbonic anhydrase facilitates this reaction.
[Image of parietal cell HCl secretion mechanism]

column1: The phenomenon of {{c1::alkaline pH in the veins::observation}} after eating is caused by the exchange of {{c2::HCO3- (bicarbonate)::ion}} for Cl- across the basolateral membrane of parietal cells [cite: 207].
column2: This is known as the 'alkaline tide'.

column1: In the production of gastric acid, {{c1::Cl- (chloride)::ion}} moves into the stomach through channels, while {{c2::H+::ion}} is moved via {{c3::active transport::transport type}} [cite: 208, 209].
column2: Active transport is required because H+ is moved against a massive concentration gradient.

column1: Parietal cells have four main basolateral receptors: G ({{c1::gastrin::stimulus}}), H ({{c2::histamine::stimulus}}), Muscarinic ({{c3::ACh::stimulus}}), and S ({{c4::somatostatin::stimulus}}) [cite: 210, 211, 212, 213, 214].
column2: The G, H, and Muscarinic receptors are stimulatory, while S is inhibitory.

column1: Activation of G, H, and Muscarinic receptors leads to the insertion of {{c1::pre-formed proton pumps::structure}} into the parietal cell membrane via {{c2::second messengers::signaling}} [cite: 215].
column2: This rapid insertion allows the stomach to respond quickly to the presence of food.

column1: To treat excessive gastric acid, doctors use {{c1::antihistamines::drug class}} to inhibit H receptors or {{c2::PPIs (Proton Pump Inhibitors)::drug class}} to block the pump itself [cite: 216, 217, 218].
column2: PPIs (like omeprazole) are generally more potent than H2-blockers.

column1: The {{c1::cephalic::phase name}} phase of gastric secretion is triggered by the {{c2::idea/sight/smell::stimulus}} of food, acting through the {{c3::vagus::nerve}} nerve [cite: 219, 220].
column2:
This phase prepares the stomach for digestion before food even arrives.
[Image of cephalic gastric and intestinal phases of gastric secretion]

column1: Vagal stimulation during the cephalic phase causes the release of {{c1::ACh::neurotransmitter}} and {{c2::gastrin::hormone}}, which stimulate {{c3::ECL::cell type}} cells and increase HCl secretion [cite: 220].
column2: This is a feed-forward mechanism.

column1: The {{c1::gastric::phase name}} phase is initiated by {{c2::stretch receptors::stimulus}}, {{c3::increased pH::stimulus}}, and the presence of {{c4::semi-digested peptides::stimulus}} in the stomach [cite: 221].
column2: This phase accounts for the majority of gastric juice secretion.

column1: The {{c1::intestinal::phase name}} phase is triggered by stretch and {{c2::decreased pH::stimulus}} in the duodenum, leading to the secretion of {{c3::secretin::hormone}} and {{c4::gastric inhibitory peptides (GIP)::hormone}} [cite: 222].
column2: This phase serves to slow down gastric emptying and acid production to protect the duodenum.

column1: During the intestinal phase, the inhibition of {{c1::vagal nuclei::brain region}} and the release of inhibitory hormones result in {{c2::decreased::effect}} HCl secretion [cite: 222].
column2: This negative feedback prevents the duodenum from being overwhelmed by acid."

column1: Gut secretions 2,"4.5.1 Bile in Digestion - Comprehensive Technical Guide
Overview of Bile and Chyme Neutralization
Acidic chyme (pH 1.0-3.5) enters the duodenum from the stomach and must be neutralized to prevent mucosal damage and provide an optimal pH for enzyme activity.
Bile (pH ~7.8) and pancreatic juice (pH 8.0-8.3) provide the necessary alkaline secretions.
Fat Emulsification and Micelle Formation
1. Emulsification:
•	Bile salts and lecithin act as detergents.
•	They break large fat globules into smaller emulsion droplets (~1 micrometer).
•	This increases the total surface area for pancreatic lipase to act upon.
2. Chemical Digestion:
•	Pancreatic lipase and its co-factor, colipase, break down triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides.
3. Micelle Formation:
•	Tiny spheres (4-7 nm) called micelles are formed from bile salts, fatty acids, and monoglycerides.
•	Micelles transport these lipid-soluble products through the aqueous environment of the intestinal lumen to the epithelial surface for absorption.
Hormonal and Neuronal Regulation
Cholecystokinin (CCK):
•	Released by duodenal enteroendocrine cells in response to fat.
•	Causes gallbladder contraction and relaxation of the Hepatopancreatic Sphincter (Sphincter of Oddi).
•	Inhibits gastric churning and constricts the pyloric sphincter to slow gastric emptying.
Secretin:
•	Released in response to acidic chyme.
•	Stimulates bile ductal cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
Vagal Stimulation:
•	Parasympathetic activation (Vagus nerve) causes weak gallbladder contractions during the cephalic and gastric phases.
4.5.2 Pancreatic secretions - In-Depth Physiological Analysis
Composition of Pancreatic Juice
The exocrine pancreas secretes approximately 1000-1500 ml of fluid daily.
Acinar Cells: Produce the 'enzyme-rich' component, including proteases, amylases, and lipases.
Ductal Cells: Produce the 'bicarbonate-rich' ($HCO_3^-$) alkaline component ($pH$ 8.0-8.3) to neutralize HCl.
Enzyme Activation Cascade
To prevent autodigestion of the pancreas, proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens.
1. Enterokinase (bound to duodenal mucosa) converts Trypsinogen into active Trypsin.
2. Trypsin then activates other enzymes:
•	Procarboxypeptidase becomes Carboxypeptidase.
•	Chymotrypsinogen becomes Chymotrypsin.
Regulation of Secretion
Secretin: Stimulated by acidic chyme ($pH$ < 4.5). Acts on ductal cells to increase $HCO_3^-$ and $H_2O$.
CCK: Stimulated by fats and proteins. Acts on acinar cells to increase digestive enzyme secretion.
Vagus Nerve: Provides parasympathetic stimulation to both cell types during the early stages of a meal.
Clinical Correlation: Pancreatitis
Pathophysiology: Inappropriate activation of enzymes within the pancreas, or defective ductal secretion.
Causes: Excessive alcohol, gallstones, or ductal obstruction.
Clinical Presentation: Abdominal pain, weight loss, and steatorrhoea (oily, floating stools due to fat malabsorption).
Management: Enzyme supplements, complete alcohol abstention, and pain relief.","Bile is produced by the {{c1::liver}} and enters the digestive tract via the {{c2::common bile duct}}.
column2: This continuous production is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder during fasting. [cite: 57]

column1: Bile eventually passes through the {{c1::pancreatic duct}} and the {{c2::sphincter of Oddi}} to reach the duodenum.
column2: Coordinated relaxation of this sphincter is essential for the entry of both bile and pancreatic juice. [cite: 57]

column1: Bile is diverted for storage in the gallbladder via the {{c1::cystic duct}}.
column2: The gallbladder can concentrate bile up to tenfold by absorbing water and ions. [cite: 58]

column1: The daily secretion volume of bile is approximately {{c1::0.7-2L}}.
column2: High volumes are necessary to maintain the pool of bile salts required for fat digestion. [cite: 59]

column1: Bile pigments are primarily the waste products from the breakdown of the {{c1::haem}} component of red blood cells.
column2: Bilirubin is the most well-known pigment, which is later converted by gut bacteria. [cite: 60]

column1: The physical breakdown of large fat globules into smaller droplets is facilitated by {{c1::lecithin}} and {{c2::bile salts}}.
column2: This process increases the surface area available for enzymatic attack. [cite: 62]

column1: The high concentration of {{c1::HCO3- (bicarbonate)}} in bile makes it an {{c2::alkaline}} fluid.
column2: This helps protect the duodenal mucosa from the corrosive effects of gastric acid. [cite: 63]

column1: The process of breaking down fat into smaller droplets is known as {{c1::emulsification}}.
column2: This is a mechanical process aided by small intestine contractions. [cite: 64]

column1: An average adult processes {{c1::70-100g}} of fat per day.
column2: Efficient emulsification is required to handle this significant dietary load. [cite: 65]

column1: Small intestine contractions create fat droplets with a diameter of {{c1::0.5-1mm}}.
column2: These droplets are still significantly larger than the micelles formed later in the process. [cite: 67]

column1: Emulsified fat droplets possess a {{c1::negative charge}}, which causes them to {{c2::repel}} each other.
column2: This electrical charge is a critical physical barrier against the coalescence of fat. [cite: 68]

column1: {{c1::Bile salts}} and {{c2::lecithin}} function as stabilizers that prevent droplets from {{c3::coalescing}}.
column2: They coat the droplets, ensuring the negative charges remain exposed to the aqueous environment. [cite: 69]

column1: Chemical digestion of fats is primarily performed by the enzyme {{c1::pancreatic lipase}}.
column2: Lipase acts at the oil-water interface of the emulsified droplets. [cite: 70]

column1: The essential cofactor {{c1::colipase}} works by {{c2::pushing away bile salts and lecithin}}, allowing lipase to access the fat.
column2: Without colipase, bile salts would actually inhibit lipase by blocking its binding site. [cite: 71]

column1: Fats are broken down into {{c1::monoglycerides}} and {{c2::fatty acids}} before they {{c3::diffuse}} through the mucosal layer of the small intestine.
column2: Passive diffusion is the primary transport mechanism for these lipophilic molecules. [cite: 72]

column1: {{c1::Micelles}} are tiny fat droplets that facilitate the transport of lipids to the intestinal wall for absorption.
column2: They are much smaller than emulsified droplets and contain a core of monoglycerides and fatty acids. [cite: 73]

column1: Acidity in the duodenum triggers the release of {{c1::secretin}}, which then stimulates {{c2::alkaline secretion}} in the bile ductal cells.
column2: This hormonal response helps regulate the pH of the intestinal contents. [cite: 75]

column1: Fats in the duodenum trigger the release of {{c1::CCK (cholecystokinin)}}.
column2: CCK is the primary hormonal regulator of gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme release. [cite: 76]

column1: CCK causes the {{c1::contraction}} of the gallbladder and the simultaneous {{c2::relaxation}} of the sphincter of Oddi.
column2: This dual action ensures that stored bile is forcefully expelled into the duodenum. [cite: 76]

column1: CCK stimulates the release of both {{c1::pancreatic lipase}} and its cofactor {{c2::colipase}}.
column2: This ensures that the enzymes needed for fat digestion arrive at the same time as the bile. [cite: 76]

column1: By inhibiting {{c1::churning in the stomach}}, CCK acts to {{c2::slow down}} gastric emptying.
column2: This feedback prevents the small intestine from being overwhelmed by too much fat at once. [cite: 76]

column1: CCK causes the {{c1::constriction}} of the pyloric sphincter.
column2: This mechanical closure prevents further chyme from entering the duodenum until current contents are processed. [cite: 76]

column1: Pancreatic secretions are overall {{c1::alkaline}} in nature.
column2: This basic pH is essential for neutralizing gastric acid and optimizing enzyme activity. [cite: 77]

column1: {{c1::Endocrine}} glands are described as {{c2::ductless}} because they empty their secretions directly into the bloodstream.
column2: The Islets of Langerhans are the endocrine component of the pancreas. [cite: 78, 79]

column1: The endocrine pancreas secretes {{c1::insulin}} and {{c2::glucagon}} to regulate blood glucose levels.
column2: Insulin lowers blood sugar, while glucagon raises it. [cite: 80]

column1: {{c1::Exocrine}} glands in the pancreas empty their secretions into the {{c2::pancreatic ducts}}.
column2: This represents about 98-99% of the pancreatic mass. [cite: 81, 82]

column1: Pancreatic {{c1::ductal}} cells secrete alkaline fluid to neutralize {{c2::chyme}}.
column2: Neutralization is required because {{c3::micelles}} require alkaline conditions to form properly. [cite: 83]

column1: Pancreatic {{c1::acinar}} cells are responsible for secreting enzymes stored in {{c2::zymogen granules}}.
column2: Zymogen granules are specialized storage vesicles that keep enzymes inactive until release. [cite: 84]

column1: Proteolytic enzymes are secreted as {{c1::inactive precursors}} to ensure they do not {{c2::digest the pancreas}}.
column2: This is a vital protective measure against pancreatic tissue damage. [cite: 85, 86]

column1: The three specific proteolytic precursors mentioned are {{c1::trypsinogen}}, {{c2::chymotrypsin}}, and {{c3::elastase}}.
column2: These are all 'pro-enzymes' that require activation in the gut. [cite: 87]

column1: The conversion of {{c1::trypsinogen}} to {{c2::trypsin}} is mediated by {{c3::enterokinase}}.
column2: Enterokinase is a brush-border enzyme found on the membrane of duodenal cells. [cite: 88]

column1: Once formed, {{c1::trypsin}} acts as the activator for all other pancreatic proteolytic precursors.
column2: This creates a chain reaction that rapidly provides active enzymes for protein digestion. [cite: 89]

column1: Apart from lipase, {{c1::cholesterolesterase}} and {{c2::phospholipase}} are also pancreatic enzymes involved in fat digestion.
column2: These enzymes break down complex lipids and cholesterol esters. [cite: 91]

column1: {{c1::Alpha amylase}} is the pancreatic enzyme that breaks down {{c2::carbohydrates}}.
column2: It targets starch molecules, continuing the digestion started by saliva. [cite: 92]

column1: {{c1::Ribonuclease}} and {{c2::deoxyribonuclease}} are secreted by the pancreas to break down {{c3::nucleic acids}}.
column2: This allows the body to recycle nucleotides from dietary DNA and RNA. [cite: 93]

column1: The release of {{c1::secretin}} into the blood is triggered specifically by {{c2::acidic chyme}} in the duodenum.
column2: Secretin is often called 'nature's antacid.' [cite: 95]

column1: The release of {{c1::cholecystokinin (CCK)}} into the blood is triggered specifically by {{c2::fatty chyme}} in the duodenum.
column2: This hormone targets both the gallbladder and the pancreatic acini. [cite: 96]

column1: {{c1::Secretin}} targets pancreatic {{c2::ductal}} cells to induce the secretion of alkaline fluid.
column2: This fluid is rich in bicarbonate ions. [cite: 97]

column1: {{c1::CCK}} targets pancreatic {{c2::acinar}} cells to induce the secretion of {{c3::pancreatic enzymes}}.
column2: This ensures that digestive enzymes are present when fat and protein are detected. [cite: 98]

column1: In the disease {{c1::pancreatitis}}, enzymes are activated in the {{c2::pancreas}} rather than the duodenum.
column2: This premature activation causes severe tissue inflammation and damage. [cite: 99, 103]

column1: A common clinical consequence of pancreatitis is that the {{c1::pH}} in the duodenum will not be {{c2::high enough}}.
column2: Low pH impairs micelle formation and inhibits the activity of any remaining enzymes. [cite: 101]

column1: Pancreatitis results in a significant {{c1::decrease}} in the total quantity of secreted enzymes.
column2: This leads to generalized maldigestion of all macronutrients. [cite: 102]

column1: The most significant risk factor for chronic pancreatitis is {{c1::excessive alcohol consumption}}.
column2: Alcohol acts as a direct toxin to pancreatic cells and alters secretion composition. [cite: 104]

column1: Symptoms of pancreatitis include {{c1::abdominal pain}}, {{c2::weight loss}}, and {{c3::malabsorption of fats}}.
column2: Pain is often severe and radiates to the back, while fat malabsorption leads to weight loss. [cite: 106, 107, 108]"

column1: Bile synthesis and the enterohepatic circulation,"5.3 Bile synthesis and the enterohepatic circulation
Introduction and Key Concepts

Bile is a complex fluid essential for the digestion and absorption of dietary lipids and the excretion of various metabolites and toxins [cite: 52]. This lesson focuses on the composition of bile, its synthesis and secretion by hepatocytes, and the intricate regulatory mechanisms governing its flow through the biliary system to the duodenum [cite: 21, 22]. A critical component of this process is the enterohepatic circulation, which ensures the efficient recycling and physiological conservation of bile salts [cite: 23].
Anatomy of the Biliary Tree
The biliary tree is a sophisticated network of ducts responsible for transporting bile from the liver to the small intestine [cite: 34].
Intrahepatic Biliary Tree

This network begins within the liver with bile canaliculi—narrow channels formed between neighboring hepatocytes [cite: 72]. These merge into ductules and eventually form the right and left hepatic ducts [cite: 34].
Extrahepatic Biliary Tree

Outside the liver, the right and left hepatic ducts join to form the common hepatic duct [cite: 34]. This duct connects to the gallbladder via the cystic duct for storage and concentration [cite: 80, 89].
Bile Synthesis and Secretion
Total daily bile flow is approximately 600 ml [cite: 53]. This volume is derived from two primary cellular sources:
•	Hepatocytes (75%): These cells synthesize primary bile acids from cholesterol [cite: 53, 140].
•	Cholangiocytes (25%): These cells modify bile as it travels through the ducts [cite: 53, 136].
Hepatocellular Secretion Mechanisms
Bile formation in the hepatocytes is an active process involving specialized transport proteins on both the basolateral (sinusoidal) and apical (canalicular) membranes [cite: 133].
•	Active Transport: Bile salts are actively transported against their concentration gradient [cite: 131].
•	Osmotic Gradient: Water moves down the concentration gradient created by secreted solutes [cite: 134].
•	Canalicular Motility: Canaliculi possess contractile properties to propel bile [cite: 73].
Bile Modification and Storage
Cholangiocyte Modification
Cholangiocytes dilute and alkalinize the bile by secreting bicarbonate (HCO3-) and water, while reabsorbing glucose and amino acids [cite: 136].
The Gallbladder
Bile is stored in the gallbladder until digestive stimuli (cholecystokinin) trigger contraction and flow into the duodenum [cite: 39, 90].
Physiological Functions of Bile
•	Fat Emulsification: Bile salts and phospholipids emulsify dietary fat, increasing surface area for enzymes [cite: 141].
•	Micelle Formation: They facilitate the formation of micelles which solubilize lipids for absorption [cite: 141].
•	Excretion: Bile aids with the excretion of various metabolites and toxins [cite: 52].
Clinical Considerations: Obstructed Bile Flow
•	Cholelithiasis: Stones form when substances like cholesterol and bilirubin become supersaturated and precipitate [cite: 99].
•	Cholecystitis: Stasis of bile in the gallbladder predisposes it to infection [cite: 117, 118].

•	Malabsorption: Lack of bile in the duodenum causes fat malabsorption and vitamin deficiency [cite: 119].","Bile is synthesized by {{c1::hepatocytes}} (75%) and {{c2::cholangiocytes::cells on the duct wall}} (25%). [cite: 3]

column1: The anatomical flow of bile begins at the {{c1::biliary canaliculi}}, moves to ductules, then the hepatic ducts, and finally the {{c2::common bile duct}}. [cite: 4]
