column1: {{c1::Sinusoids}} are specialized liver capillaries that receive blood from both the {{c2::hepatic artery}} and the {{c3::portal vein}}. [cite: 6]
column2: This dual blood supply ensures the liver receives both oxygenated blood and nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract. [cite: 6]

column1: The portal vein carries blood from the {{c1::GI system}}, which is specifically rich in {{c2::nutrients}}. [cite: 7]
column2: This allows the liver to process absorbed substances immediately before they enter systemic circulation. [cite: 7]

column1: Liver sinusoids have a {{c1::discontinuous}} endothelium, which facilitates the exchange of substances with {{c2::hepatocytes}}. [cite: 8]
column2: This ""leaky"" structure is essential for high-volume metabolic exchange and protein transport. [cite: 8]

column1: {{c1::Bile canaliculi}} are located in the space between {{c2::hepatocytes}}, making secretion efficient. [cite: 9, 10]
column2: The proximity allows for direct transport of bile components from the cell to the drainage system. [cite: 10]

column1: Bile canaliculi possess {{c1::microvilli}} and {{c2::contractile properties}} to aid in the movement of bile. [cite: 11]
column2: This active movement prevents stasis at the microscopic level before bile reaches the larger ductules. [cite: 11]

column1: The gallbladder's primary function is {{c1::storing}} bile, which occurs when the {{c2::Ampulla of Vater}} is closed. [cite: 12, 13]
column2: This allows bile to be concentrated and saved for when a meal is actually consumed. [cite: 13]

column1: The hormone {{c1::Cholecystokinin (CCK)}} acts as the primary trigger to release bile from the gallbladder. [cite: 14]
column2: CCK is released by the duodenum in response to fats and proteins entering the small intestine. [cite: 14]

column1: The two main purposes of bile are the {{c1::digestion of fat}} and the {{c2::excretion of metabolites/toxins}}. [cite: 15, 16, 17]
column2: Bile acts as both a digestive secretion and an essential excretory route for waste products like bilirubin. [cite: 16, 17]

column1: Gallstones are typically caused by an excess of {{c1::cholesterol}} or {{c2::bilirubin}} in the bile. [cite: 18, 19]
column2: When these substances become supersaturated, they precipitate into solids, which can then block the biliary tree. [cite: 19, 20]

column1: Biliary obstruction can be caused by {{c1::strictures::narrowing}} of the duct or {{c2::external tumors}}. [cite: 21, 22, 23]
column2: A classic clinical example of an external growth is cancer of the {{c3::head of the pancreas}}. [cite: 23]

column1: Stasis of bile in the gallbladder due to obstruction can lead to {{c1::inflammation}} and {{c2::infection}}. [cite: 24, 25]
column2: Prolonged stasis is a major risk factor for acute cholecystitis or cholangitis. [cite: 25]

column1: Bile flow obstruction leads to {{c1::dilated}} bile ducts due to the pressure of {{c2::backflow}}. [cite: 26]
column2: This dilation can often be visualized via ultrasound or CT imaging to confirm the site of obstruction. [cite: 26]

column1: Failure to digest fats due to obstruction results in {{c1::steatorrhea::fatty stools}} and deficiencies in fat-soluble vitamins {{c2::A, D, and K}}. [cite: 27]
column2: Vitamin E is also fat-soluble, though Vitamin K deficiency is often most acute due to its role in coagulation. [cite: 27]

column1: Bile formation requires components to be either made in or transported through the {{c1::hepatocyte}} before entering the {{c2::bile duct}}. [cite: 28, 29, 30]
column2: This process ensures that substances from the sinusoids are processed before excretion. [cite: 30]

column1: The transport of most bile components into the hepatocyte and then into bile requires {{c1::active transport}} using multiple {{c2::carriers}}. [cite: 31]
column2: This energy-dependent process allows for the movement of substances against their concentration gradients. [cite: 31]

column1: Cholangiocytes contribute to bile modification by allowing {{c1::water}} to enter, which {{c2::dilutes}} the bile. [cite: 32, 33]
column2: This modification occurs as the bile moves from the liver through the ductal system. [cite: 33]

column1: Cholangiocytes secrete {{c1::bicarbonate}}, which {{c2::alkalinizes}} the bile to help neutralise {{c3::acidic chyme}}. [cite: 34]
column2: This alkaline environment is also essential for the optimal activity of pancreatic enzymes. [cite: 34]

column1: Bile acids are synthesized from {{c1::cholesterol}}. [cite: 35, 36]
column2: Cholesterol is the precursor for all primary bile acids produced in the liver. [cite: 36]

column1: The two main types of primary bile acids are {{c1::cholic acid}} and {{c2::chenodeoxycholic acid}}. [cite: 37]
column2: These are synthesized by hepatocytes and are the building blocks of bile salts. [cite: 37]

column1: A bile acid becomes a **bile salt** when it is {{c1::conjugated}} with an {{c2::amino acid}}. [cite: 38, 39]
column2: Conjugation makes the molecule more water-soluble and effective at physiological pH. [cite: 39]

column1: Bile salts and phospholipids are essential for {{c1::fat emulsification}} by breaking large fat droplets into {{c2::micelles}}. [cite: 41, 42]
column2: This physical breakdown dramatically increases the surface area available for lipase to act upon. [cite: 42]

column1: Bile salts are amphipathic, meaning they have a {{c1::hydrophobic}} side that attaches to fat and a {{c2::hydrophilic}} side that faces the aqueous environment. [cite: 43, 44]
column2: This property allows them to stabilize small fat droplets in the watery contents of the intestine. [cite: 44]

column1: The process of recycling bile salts is known as {{c1::enterohepatic circulation}}. [cite: 45, 46]
column2: This efficient system minimizes the amount of new cholesterol the liver needs to synthesize daily. [cite: 46]

column1: Bile salts are reabsorbed in the {{c1::terminal ileum}} via the process of {{c2::active transport}}. [cite: 47]
column2: Damage to this specific part of the small intestine can lead to bile acid malabsorption and diarrhea. [cite: 47]

column1: After reabsorption in the terminal ileum, bile salts travel back to the liver via the {{c1::portal vein}}. [cite: 48]
column2: This completes the recycling loop, allowing the salts to be secreted again into the bile. [cite: 48]"

column1: Jaundice,"Investigations of Jaundice
Definition and Pathophysiology

Jaundice (icterus) is the yellowing of the skin and sclerae due to the deposition of excess bilirubin. Bilirubin has a high affinity for elastin, which is why it is often first noticed in the sclera of the eye.
It occurs when there is an imbalance between bilirubin production and excretion, leading to hyperbilirubinemia.
Bilirubin Metabolism Overview
1. Synthesis: Breakdown of senescent erythrocytes by mononuclear phagocytic cells (Heme -> Biliverdin -> Unconjugated Bilirubin).
2. Transport: Unconjugated bilirubin (insoluble) travels to the liver bound to albumin.
3. Conjugation: In the hepatocyte, bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid (via UGT1A1) to become water-soluble.
4. Excretion: Secreted into bile and enters the gut, where it is converted to urobilinogen and stercobilin (giving stool its color).
Classification of Jaundice
Pre-hepatic: Overproduction of bilirubin (e.g., hemolytic anemia). Findings: High unconjugated bilirubin, dark stool/urine (due to high urobilinogen), normal LFTs.
Intra-hepatic: Liver damage or enzyme deficiency (e.g., Hepatitis, Cirrhosis, Gilbert's). Findings: Mixed conjugated/unconjugated bilirubin, elevated ALT/AST.

Post-hepatic (Obstructive): Obstruction of bile flow (e.g., gallstones, pancreatic cancer). Findings: High conjugated bilirubin, tea-colored urine (conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble), pale/clay-colored stools (no stercobilin), elevated ALP/GGT.","Jaundice is clinically defined as having too much {{c1::bilirubin}} in the blood. [cite: 2]
column2: Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced during the normal breakdown of red blood cells.

column1: The two primary mechanisms that cause jaundice are the {{c1::overproduction}} of bilirubin or the {{c2::inability to excrete}} it. [cite: 3, 4]
column2: These categories help clinicians differentiate between pre-hepatic and post-hepatic issues.

column1: Jaundice is visually observed as yellowing of the skin and eyes because bilirubin has a high affinity for {{c1::elastin}}. [cite: 6, 7]
column2: This is why the sclera of the eye is often the first place jaundice becomes visible.

column1: Bilirubin is synthesized from the {{c1::heme group}} of old red blood cells. [cite: 9]
column2: Hemoglobin is broken down into heme and globin; heme is the precursor to bile pigments.

column1: The first step of heme degradation occurs in the {{c1::reticuloendothelial system::type of phagocytes}}, producing {{c2::biliverdin}}. [cite: 10]
column2: This system includes the spleen and liver.

column1: In the synthesis pathway, {{c1::biliverdin}} is converted into {{c2::bilirubin}}. [cite: 11]
column2: This happens before the bilirubin is transported to the liver.

column1: {{c1::Unconjugated}} bilirubin is lipid-soluble and potentially {{c2::neurotoxic}}. [cite: 12]
column2: Because it is lipid-soluble, it can cross cell membranes, including the blood-brain barrier in certain conditions.

column1: Bilirubin undergoes conjugation in the {{c1::liver}} using {{c2::glucuronic acid}}. [cite: 13, 14]
column2: This process is essential for making the pigment excretable.

column1: After conjugation, bilirubin becomes {{c1::water soluble}}, which allows it to enter the {{c2::gut::organ}}. [cite: 15, 16]
column2: Prior to this, it was lipid-soluble and required a transport protein (albumin).

column1: In the gut, conjugated bilirubin is processed by {{c1::intestinal bacteria}} into {{c2::urobilinogen}}. [cite: 18]
column2: This is a key step in the excretory function of the liver.

column1: Pre-hepatic jaundice is primarily {{c1::hemolytic}} in nature, caused by excessive RBC breakdown. [cite: 19, 20]
column2: This results in the liver being overwhelmed by the sheer volume of heme groups.

column1: Patients with pre-hepatic jaundice typically present with a {{c1::lemon yellow}} discoloration and look {{c2::pale}}. [cite: 21]
column2: The pallor is usually due to the underlying anemia from hemolysis.

column1: A structural RBC defect that can cause pre-hepatic jaundice is {{c1::spherocytosis}}, where cells are too {{c2::big and globular}}. [cite: 23]
column2: These abnormal cells are trapped and destroyed by the spleen.

column1: {{c1::G6PD deficiency}} is a common enzyme deficiency that leads to pre-hepatic jaundice. [cite: 24]
column2: This enzyme is crucial for protecting RBCs from oxidative damage.

column1: Pre-hepatic jaundice is characterized by an excess of {{c1::unconjugated}} bilirubin and excess {{c2::urobilinogen}} in the blood. [cite: 25, 26]
column2: Urobilinogen is elevated because the liver is working at maximum capacity to conjugate the excess heme.

column1: Hepatic jaundice occurs when the {{c1::conjugation}} process is disrupted or bilirubin cannot enter the {{c2::hepatocyte}}. [cite: 28, 29]
column2: This is fundamentally a problem with the liver's internal machinery.

column1: Hepatic jaundice most commonly occurs when {{c1::hepatocytes}} are damaged. [cite: 30]
column2: Rare enzyme deficiencies can also cause this, but cellular damage is the primary driver.

column1: Specific pathologies that lead to hepatic jaundice include {{c1::fatty liver}}, {{c2::fibrosis}}, and {{c3::cirrhosis}}. [cite: 35, 36, 37]
column2: These conditions represent varying stages and types of liver tissue damage.

column1: In hepatic jaundice, the bilirubin found in the blood could be {{c1::conjugated or unconjugated}}. [cite: 33]
column2: This depends on whether the damage affects the uptake of bilirubin or its secretion from the cell.

column1: Post-hepatic jaundice is caused by the {{c1::obstruction}} of bile flow, leading to a {{c2::backflow}} into the blood. [cite: 39, 40]
column2: This is often called ""obstructive jaundice.""

column1: Post-hepatic jaundice is characterized by high levels of {{c1::conjugated}} bilirubin in the blood. [cite: 41]
column2: Since the liver has already processed the bilirubin, it is water-soluble.

column1: A classic sign of post-hepatic jaundice is {{c1::tea-coloured}} urine. [cite: 42]
column2: This occurs because the water-soluble conjugated bilirubin is filtered and excreted by the kidneys.

column1: Patients with post-hepatic jaundice often have {{c1::pale stools}} because there is no {{c2::stercobilin}} reaching the gut. [cite: 43]
column2: Stercobilin is the pigment derived from bilirubin that normally browns the stool.

column1: The most common cause of post-hepatic jaundice is {{c1::gallstones}}. [cite: 45]
column2: These stones block the common bile duct, preventing the exit of bile.

column1: The investigation known as {{c1::ERCP::acronym}} involves putting a probe in to visualize the bile ducts. [cite: 46]
column2: It stands for Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography.

column1: Neonatal jaundice occurs because newborns have more {{c1::haemoglobin}} than adults and undergo significant {{c2::haemolysis}}. [cite: 48]
column2: This is part of the transition from fetal to adult physiology.

column1: Neonatal jaundice is often considered normal in the first few days because the {{c1::liver system}} is still immature. [cite: 49]
column2: However, extreme levels are dangerous due to the neurotoxicity of unconjugated bilirubin.

column1: Severe neonatal jaundice can cause {{c1::kernicterus}}, which is damage to the {{c2::basal ganglia}}. [cite: 50, 51]
column2: This happens because the infant's blood-brain barrier is not yet fully developed.

column1: Elevated blood levels of {{c1::AST and ALT}} enzymes suggest {{c2::intrahepatic (hepatic)}} jaundice. [cite: 55, 56]
column2: These enzymes are released from the cytoplasm of damaged hepatocytes.

column1: {{c1::Cholestasis}} is the term for the backflow of bile, which typically indicates {{c2::post-hepatic}} jaundice. [cite: 57]
column2: It is identified by specific enzyme markers on a Liver Function Test.

column1: Elevated levels of {{c1::ALP and GGT}} on an LFT indicate cholestasis or post-hepatic jaundice. [cite: 58]
column2: These enzymes are associated with the biliary tree.

column1: To assess the {{c1::synthetic function}} of the liver, clinicians check levels of {{c2::albumin}} and {{c3::clotting factors}}. [cite: 59, 60]
column2: Because the liver produces these, low levels indicate severe, chronic liver damage.

column1: Urinalysis for jaundice patients checks for the presence of {{c1::urobilinogen}} and {{c2::conjugated bilirubin}}. [cite: 61]
column2: Unconjugated bilirubin will not appear in urine because it is lipid-soluble.

column1: In liver pathology, increased levels of {{c1::oestrogen}} can lead to {{c2::enlarged breasts (gynecomastia)}} and {{c3::spider naevi}}. [cite: 64, 65, 66]
column2: The liver is responsible for metabolizing steroid hormones like estrogen.

column1: {{c1::Spider naevi}} and {{c2::palmar erythema}} in liver patients are caused by {{c3::vasodilation}}. [cite: 66, 67]
column2: This is a secondary effect of hormone imbalances caused by liver failure.

column1: Low albumin levels in liver disease lead to the clinical symptom of {{c1::edema}}. [cite: 68]
column2: This is due to the loss of plasma oncotic pressure.

column1: An enlarged spleen in liver disease is usually caused by {{c1::blood flow obstruction}}. [cite: 69]
column2: This occurs when portal hypertension forces blood back into the splenic vein.

column1: Patients with liver disease may experience easy {{c1::bruising}} because the liver is producing fewer {{c2::clotting factors}}. [cite: 71]
column2: This is a critical sign of impaired synthetic function.

column1: To test for metabolic liver diseases, clinicians check for {{c1::copper}} (Wilson's disease) or {{c2::ferritin}} (hemochromatosis). [cite: 75]
column2: These tests look for the accumulation of specific metals in the body.

column1: If {{c1::hepatitis}} is suspected as the cause of jaundice, the appropriate investigation is {{c2::serology}}. [cite: 73]
column2: This looks for viral antigens or antibodies in the blood."

column1: Infection of the gut,"Infections of the Gastrointestinal Tract
Background
GIT infections are a major cause of global morbidity. Pathogens are primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route and can cause disease through invasion or toxin production.
Bacterial Pathogens
Salmonella: Associated with poultry/eggs. S. typhi causes systemic Typhoid fever.
Campylobacter: Most common bacterial cause of diarrhea in many regions.
Vibrio cholerae: Causes profuse 'rice-water' stool through toxin-mediated disruption of ion transport.
E. coli: Various strains (ETEC, EHEC/STEC) range from traveler's diarrhea to hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
Shigella: Highly infectious; causes bacillary dysentery (bloody diarrhea).
Specific Conditions
Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: Disruption of flora allows C. difficile to multiply, potentially causing pseudomembranous colitis.
Food Poisoning: Ingestion of pre-formed toxins (S. aureus, B. cereus) often results in rapid onset vomiting.
Helicobacter pylori: Colonizes the stomach, causing chronic gastritis and increasing risk for peptic ulcers and gastric cancer.
Viral Gastroenteritis
Norovirus: Common in all ages, often causes outbreaks in closed communities (cruises, schools).

Rotavirus: Primarily affects infants and young children; significant cause of childhood dehydration globally.","When taking a clinical history for GI issues, it is important to check for {{c1::travel}} [cite: 3], {{c2::activities}} (e.g., bushwalking) [cite: 4], and {{c3::food/restaurants}} [cite: 5].
column2: These factors help identify environmental or behavioral risk factors for infection.

column1: In patients with gastrointestinal symptoms, practitioners should first rule out {{c1::infectious}} causes [cite: 7].
column2: This is a primary diagnostic priority before considering non-infectious pathologies.

column1: When assessing immune status for GI risk, specific attention should be paid to {{c1::chemotherapy}} or recent {{c2::surgery}} [cite: 8].
column2: Immunocompromised patients are susceptible to a wider range of opportunistic pathogens.

column1: {{c1::High volume::Stool characteristic}} diarrhoea typically indicates that the source of the problem is in the {{c2::small intestine}} [cite: 11].
column2: Contrast this with small-volume, frequent stools often associated with the large intestine.

column1: {{c1::Dysentery}} is a condition characterized by damage in the GIT resulting in {{c2::blood and pus}} in the stool [cite: 13, 14, 15].
column2: It is also commonly associated with pain and fever [cite: 16].

column1: Non-typhoidal Salmonella is typically transmitted to humans from {{c1::animals}} [cite: 17, 18].
column2: This zoonotic pathogen usually causes self-limiting illness [cite: 20].

column1: The infectious dose required for a {{c1::non-typhoidal Salmonella::pathogen}} infection is approximately {{c2::10^5}} organisms [cite: 19].
column2: Treatment primarily focuses on fluid and electrolyte replacement [cite: 21].

column1: One pitfall of using antibiotics for non-typhoidal Salmonella is that they can {{c1::wipe out normal intestinal bacteria}} [cite: 22].
column2: This can prolong the carrier state or lead to dysbiosis.

column1: Salmonella typhoidal, the cause of {{c1::enteric fever}}, is uniquely passed only between {{c2::humans}} [cite: 23, 24, 29].
column2: Unlike non-typhoidal strains, there is no animal reservoir.

column1: A classic clinical sign of Salmonella typhoidal (enteric fever) is the appearance of {{c1::rose spots}} on the skin [cite: 26].
column2: This occurs after a notably long incubation period [cite: 25].

column1: Salmonella typhoidal pathogens invade {{c1::M cells}} in the gut to reach and multiply inside {{c2::macrophages}} [cite: 27].
column2: This intracellular lifestyle is key to its pathogenesis and systemic spread.

column1: The definitive method to diagnose Salmonella typhoidal is via a {{c1::blood culture}} [cite: 28].
column2: This is necessary because the pathogen becomes systemic.

column1: The Enterobacteriaceae group, which includes E. coli and Salmonella, are morphologically identified as {{c1::Gram-negative rods}} [cite: 30, 40].
column2: This is a fundamental microbiological classification for these GI pathogens.

column1: {{c1::Enterotoxigenic}} E. coli (ETEC) is a variety of E. coli particularly common in {{c2::travellers}} [cite: 33, 34].
column2: It is a leading cause of 'Traveler\'s Diarrhea'.

column1: {{c1::Enterohaemorrhagic}} E. coli (EHEC) is dangerous because it can lead to {{c2::kidney failure}} [cite: 35, 36].
column2: This is often due to the production of Shiga-like toxins (HUS).

column1: {{c1::Enteroinvasive::E. coli type}} E. coli (EIEC) is known for its ability to cause {{c2::dysentery}} [cite: 37, 38].
column2: It mimics Shigella in its clinical presentation.

column1: In Cholera, the intestinal wall {{c1::pumps out water}}, leading to the characteristic {{c2::rice-water stool}} [cite: 41, 42].
column2: Vibrio cholerae is a Gram-negative bacterium that often lives in fresh water [cite: 43, 45].

column1: The mechanism of the Cholera toxin involves tricking epithelial cells into increasing {{c1::cAMP::second messenger}}, which increases the release of {{c2::electrolytes}} [cite: 46].
column2: This osmotic shift causes massive water loss into the intestinal lumen.

column1: {{c1::Shigella}} is highly infectious, requiring only {{c2::10}} organisms to cause disease [cite: 48, 50].
column2: It causes dysentery where watery diarrhoea progresses to mucus and blood [cite: 49, 51].

column1: {{c1::Campylobacter}} grows optimally at a temperature of {{c2::42}} degrees Celsius [cite: 53, 54].
column2: It is often acquired from contaminated food and causes inflammation, bleeding, and ulcerations [cite: 55, 56].

column1: Pathogens like Campylobacter utilize {{c1::cytotoxins}} and {{c2::local invasion}} to damage the gut [cite: 57, 58].
column2: This distinguishes it from purely toxigenic infections like Cholera.

column1: Deep invasion of the GI tract is characteristic of {{c1::Amoebiasis}} [cite: 60, 61].
column2: This can lead to more severe systemic complications than superficial infections.

column1: Other systemic infections that involve the GI tract or enteric route include {{c1::Hepatitis A}} and {{c2::enteric fevers}} [cite: 62, 63].
column2: These often present with constitutional symptoms alongside GI signs.

column1: Damage to the mucosal epithelium can occur from previous infection or {{c1::surgery}}, potentially leading to {{c2::peritonitis}} or abscesses [cite: 64, 65, 66].
column2: Such structural damage compromises the gut barrier.

column1: The primary bacterial cause of gastric ulcers is {{c1::Helicobacter pylori::H. pylori}} [cite: 67, 68].
column2: It is a Gram-negative spiral bacteria [cite: 102].

column1: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea is often caused by the multiplication of {{c1::Clostridioides difficile::C. diff}} [cite: 69, 70].
column2: It produces toxins that increase intestinal permeability and cause tissue necrosis in the colon [cite: 71, 72, 73].

column1: Food poisoning is strictly defined as the ingestion of {{c1::pre-formed toxins}} on food [cite: 74, 75].
column2: Unlike infections, these toxins act within hours of ingestion [cite: 77].

column1: {{c1::Staphylococcus aureus::S. aureus}} is a common cause of food poisoning, with {{c2::50%}} of people carrying it in their nose or on their skin [cite: 78, 79].
column2: It produces a heat-stable enterotoxin [cite: 80].

column1: {{c1::Bacillus cereus}} is a Gram-positive, spore-forming bacterium often associated with {{c2::fried rice}} [cite: 81, 82, 83, 85].
column2: Its spores can survive the cooking process [cite: 84].

column1: Bacillus cereus produces two types of enterotoxins: an {{c1::emetic}} form (acting in 15m-4hr) and a {{c2::diarrhoeal}} form (acting in 8-12hr) [cite: 86, 87, 88].
column2: The emetic form is rapid-onset due to pre-formed toxin.

column1: {{c1::Clostridium botulinum}} produces exotoxins that are anaerobic and cause {{c2::flaccid muscle paralysis}} [cite: 89, 90, 91, 93].
column2: The paralysis typically moves downwards and is fatal if it reaches the diaphragm [cite: 94].

column1: {{c1::Clostridium perfringens}} is an anaerobic Gram-positive organism that forms {{c2::spores}} [cite: 95, 96, 97].
column2: While usually self-limiting, severe cases can cause necrosis of the small bowel [cite: 99, 100].

column1: Helicobacter pylori utilizes the {{c1::urease}} enzyme to convert urea into {{c2::ammonium}} and CO2 [cite: 101, 105, 106].
column2: This process increases the local pH, allowing the bacteria to survive gastric acid.

column1: By increasing the pH, H. pylori makes the gastric mucin {{c1::less viscous}}, allowing the bacteria to reach {{c2::epithelial cells}} [cite: 107].
column2: This leads to ulcers and potentially gastric cancer [cite: 103].

column1: Two non-invasive tests for detecting H. pylori include the {{c1::breath test}} and the {{c2::faecal antigen test}} [cite: 108, 109, 110].
column2: These avoid the need for endoscopy in many cases.

column1: {{c1::Norovirus}} is a common cause of viral diarrhoea/vomiting that is self-limiting within {{c2::24-48}} hours [cite: 111, 112, 113].
column2: It has an incubation period of 12-72 hours [cite: 114].

column1: {{c1::Rotavirus}} infection is most common in infants aged {{c2::6 months to 2 years}} [cite: 115, 116].
column2: Its symptoms can last up to 7 days [cite: 119].

column1: Breastfeeding provides protection against Rotavirus through the transfer of {{c1::IgA}} antibodies [cite: 117].
column2: This maternal immunity is crucial for protecting young infants."

column1: Drugs affecting GIT motility,"Drugs Affecting Gut Motility
Treatment of Constipation (Purgatives)
Bulk-forming laxatives: Fiber-based; retain water in the gut (e.g., Psyllium).
Osmotic laxatives: Draw water into the lumen via osmosis (e.g., Lactulose, Magnesium salts).
Stimulant laxatives: Increase peristalsis by irritating the mucosa (e.g., Senna, Bisacodyl).
Stool softeners: Detergent-like action to help water penetrate stools (e.g., Docusate).
Treatment of Diarrhea
Antimotility agents: Opioid agonists (e.g., Loperamide) activate mu-receptors in the GIT to slow transit and increase water absorption.
Adsorbents: May bind toxins (e.g., Kaolin/Pectin), though evidence is limited compared to rehydration.
Nausea and Vomiting (Anti-emetics)
Vomiting is controlled by the Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ) and the Vomiting Centre.
D2 Antagonists: Metoclopramide and Domperidone; block dopamine in the CTZ and facilitate gastric emptying.
5-HT3 Antagonists: Ondansetron; highly effective for chemotherapy-induced and post-operative nausea.
NK1 Antagonists: Aprepitant; blocks Substance P and is used as an adjunct in severe emetic protocols.
Muscarinic/Histamine Antagonists: Used for motion sickness (e.g., Hyoscine, Promethazine).",
Key concepts in nutrition science,"6.4 Key concepts in nutrition science - Detailed Comprehensive Guide
Historical Evolution of Nutrition
•	Pre-WWII Era: Focus was on identifying essential nutrients to prevent deficiency diseases (e.g., Scurvy, Beriberi, Rickets). Research centered on 'minimal' requirements for survival.

•	Post-WWII Era: Shift toward 'optimal' nutrition and chronic disease prevention. The 'Nutrition Transition' marked a move toward high-energy, processed diets, leading to the rise of obesity, Type 2 Diabetes, and Cardiovascular Disease.
•	Modern Era: Focus on the 'Double Burden' of malnutrition where under-nutrition and over-nutrition coexist in the same populations or even households.
Classification of Chemical Constituents
•	Macronutrients: Required in gram quantities. Carbohydrates (17kJ/g), Protein (17kJ/g), Lipids (37kJ/g), and Alcohol (29kJ/g - though not a nutrient).
•	Micronutrients: Required in milli- or microgram quantities. Includes Vitamins (water-soluble like B-complex/C and fat-soluble like A, D, E, K) and Minerals.

•	Non-Nutrient Components: Phytochemicals (e.g., polyphenols in tea), pigments (chlorophyll, carotenoids), and additives (preservatives, flavors) which may have antioxidant or health-modulating effects but are not essential for life.
Energy Metabolism and Density
•	Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR): The energy required for basic life-sustaining functions (60-70% of TEE).
•	Thermic Effect of Food (TEF): Energy used for digestion/absorption (~10%).

•	Energy Density (ED): Calculated as Energy (kJ) / Weight (g). High ED foods (>10kJ/g) are often high in fat/sugar and low in water. Low ED foods (<6kJ/g) are typically high in water and fiber (fruits/vegetables).

•	Satiety vs. Satiation: Satiation occurs during a meal (stopping the act of eating), while satiety is the state of fullness between meals.","Protein is composed of building blocks called {{c1::amino acids}} [cite: 2, 3].
column2: **Context:** Amino acids are the organic compounds that combine to form proteins, serving as the structural components of body tissues.

column1: The human body requires {{c1::9}} essential amino acids that must be obtained via diet [cite: 4].
column2: **Context:** Essential means the body cannot synthesize these amino acids de novo or at a rate sufficient to meet demand.

column1: There are {{c1::5}} non-essential amino acids [cite: 5].
column2: **Context:** These are produced by the body naturally, meaning dietary intake is not strictly necessary for survival.

column1: There are {{c1::6}} amino acids classified as {{c2::conditional essential}} [cite: 6].
column2: **Context:** These are normally non-essential but become essential under specific physiological conditions like severe illness or metabolic stress.

column1: {{c1::Triglycerides}} represent the chemical form of both fats and oils [cite: 8].
column2: **Context:** Chemically, these consist of three fatty acids esterified to a single glycerol molecule.

column1: Saturated fats are characterized by having {{c1::no double bonds}} between carbon atoms [cite: 9].
column2: **Context:** This structural trait allows the molecules to pack tightly, usually making them solid at room temperature.

column1: The lipid class known as {{c1::sterols}} includes {{c2::cholesterol}}, which serves as a precursor for {{c3::steroids}} [cite: 10, 11].
column2: **Context:** Cholesterol is vital for cell membrane fluiditiy and the synthesis of hormones like cortisol and testosterone.

column1: {{c1::Phospholipids}} are a major lipid component of cell membranes [cite: 12].
column2: **Context:** They are amphipathic, containing both a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails, forming the lipid bilayer.

column1: Dietary fibre is defined as carbohydrates that {{c1::cannot be digested}} by humans [cite: 14, 15].
column2: **Context:** Unlike other carbs, fiber passes through the small intestine largely intact, providing bulk for stool and fuel for gut bacteria.

column1: Three specific examples of dietary fibre include {{c1::B-glucan}}, {{c2::inulin}}, and {{c3::cellulose}} [cite: 16, 17, 18].
column2: **Context:** Cellulose provides plant wall structure; Inulin is a prebiotic; B-glucan (found in oats) is known for heart health benefits.

column1: There are a total of {{c1::13}} essential vitamins [cite: 20].
column2: **Context:** These are organic micronutrients that the body needs in small quantities for various biochemical functions.

column1: Vitamins are categorized into {{c1::4}} fat-soluble and {{c2::9}} water-soluble types [cite: 21, 22].
column2: **Context:** Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K. Water-soluble: Vitamin C and the B-vitamin complex.

column1: Vitamins can be highly {{c1::sensitive to food processing}} [cite: 23].
column2: **Context:** Heat, light, oxygen, and pH changes during cooking or storage can denature or leach vitamins, reducing nutritional value.

column1: Water-soluble vitamins are absorbed directly into the {{c1::bloodstream}} [cite: 25].
column2: **Context:** Because they dissolve in water, they circulate freely but are also easily excreted by the kidneys.

column1: Fat-soluble vitamins are transported by {{c1::chylomicrons}} and typically travel through the {{c2::lymph}} system [cite: 26, 27, 28].
column2: **Context:** Chylomicrons are lipoprotein particles that consist of triglycerides, phospholipids, cholesterol, and proteins.

column1: The primary storage sites for fat-soluble vitamins are {{c1::lipoproteins}} and the {{c2::liver}} [cite: 29].
column2: **Context:** This storage capacity allows the body to maintain levels during periods of low intake but increases the risk of accumulation.

column1: {{c1::Fat-soluble}} vitamins have a higher risk of {{c2::toxicity}} because they are {{c3::less easily}} excreted by the kidneys [cite: 30, 31].
column2: **Context:** Excessive intake (hypervitaminosis) is more common with A and D than with water-soluble vitamins.

column1: Energy expenditure can be measured by the amount of {{c1::O2 (oxygen)}} breathed in and {{c2::CO2 (carbon dioxide)}} breathed out [cite: 33].
column2: **Context:** This method is called indirect calorimetry and relies on the fact that gas exchange is proportional to metabolic rate.

column1: Physical activity level (PAL) is calculated using the formula: {{c1::Total energy expenditure (TEE)}} / {{c2::Basal metabolic rate (BMR)}} [cite: 34].
column2: **Context:** PAL = $TEE/BMR$. It provides a multiplier to estimate daily caloric needs based on activity.

column1: {{c1::METs (Metabolic Equivalents)}} are a measure of the {{c2::intensity}} of physical activity [cite: 35].
column2: **Context:** 1 MET is defined as the energy cost of sitting quietly; higher values indicate more vigorous exercise.

column1: In a {{c1::positive}} energy balance, carbohydrates are converted to {{c2::glucose}} and then stored as {{c3::glycogen}} [cite: 36, 37].
column2: **Context:** Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles for quick energy access.

column1: In a positive energy balance, fats are broken down into {{c1::fatty acids + glycerol}} and stored in {{c2::adipose tissue}} [cite: 38].
column2: **Context:** Adipose tissue is the body's long-term energy reservoir.

column1: During a positive energy balance, proteins are broken down into amino acids and are {{c1::prioritised as fuel}} [cite: 39].
column2: **Context:** The body does not have a specialized storage form for protein (like glycogen or adipose), so excess is often oxidized.

column1: A {{c1::negative}} energy balance forces the body to {{c2::use its energy stores}} [cite: 40, 41].
column2: **Context:** This state occurs when energy output exceeds intake, leading to the mobilization of fat and glycogen for survival.

column1: {{c1::Fat}} has a higher energy density than both carbohydrate and protein [cite: 42].
column2: **Context:** Fat provides approx. 9 kcal/g, whereas carbs and protein provide approx. 4 kcal/g.

column1: The presence of {{c1::water}} and {{c2::fibre}} in food results in a {{c3::lower}} energy density [cite: 43].
column2: **Context:** High-water/high-fiber foods (like vegetables) allow for larger volumes of food to be consumed with fewer total calories."

column1: Nutrients in the body, deficiencies and excesses,"6.5 Nutrients in the body, deficiencies and excesses - Technical Review
Framework for Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs)
•	EAR (Estimated Average Requirement): Median daily intake level estimated to meet requirements of half the healthy individuals in a life stage/gender group.

•	RDI (Recommended Dietary Intake): EAR + 2 Standard Deviations. Designed to meet the needs of nearly all (98%) healthy individuals. Note: If EAR cannot be determined, an Adequate Intake (AI) is used.
•	UL (Upper Level of Intake): The maximum level of daily nutrient intake that is likely to pose no risk of adverse health effects to almost all individuals.
•	SDT (Suggested Dietary Target): Intakes of certain nutrients (like fiber or omega-3) that may help prevent chronic disease.
Iron Homeostasis and Deficiency

•	Bioavailability: Heme iron (animal sources) has high absorption (15-35%); Non-heme iron (plant sources) has lower absorption (2-20%) and is affected by enhancers (Vitamin C) and inhibitors (Phytates, Calcium, Tannins).
•	Iron Requirements: Men (8mg/day), Women 19-50 (18mg/day), Pregnant Women (27mg/day). Vegetarians are advised to consume 1.8x these amounts due to lower bioavailability.
•	Stages of Iron Deficiency: 1. Depleted stores (Low Ferritin); 2. Iron-deficient erythropoiesis (High Transferrin/Low Saturation); 3. Iron Deficiency Anemia (Low Hemoglobin/Hematocrit).
Clinical Deficiency Syndromes
•	Thiamin (B1): Beriberi (Wet/Dry) and Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (common in alcohol abuse).
•	Niacin (B3): Pellagra (The 4 D's: Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, Death).
•	Vitamin C: Scurvy (impaired collagen synthesis leading to bleeding gums and poor wound healing).
•	Iodine: Goitre and Cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism).","Nutrient Reference Values (NRVs) are sets of recommendations specifically designed for {{c1::healthy}} people. [cite: 4]
column2: NRVs are not intended for individuals with acute or chronic diseases which might increase or decrease their nutrient requirements. [cite: 4]

column1: The {{c1::Estimated Average Requirement (EAR)}} is the nutrient level that meets the requirements of {{c2::50%}} of individuals in a specific life stage and gender group. [cite: 5, 6]
column2: The EAR is used as a baseline to determine the RDI; by definition, it leaves half the population deficient if used as an individual goal. [cite: 5, 6]

column1: The {{c1::Recommended Dietary Intake (RDI)}} is the nutrient level that meets the requirements of {{c2::97-98%}} of healthy people. [cite: 7, 8]
column2: The RDI is calculated based on the EAR (usually EAR + 2 standard deviations) to ensure nearly the entire population is covered. [cite: 7, 8]

column1: {{c1::Adequate Intake (AI)}} is a nutrient level used when an {{c2::RDI}} cannot be determined, based on levels that seem to keep healthy people healthy. [cite: 9, 10, 11]
column2: AI is an estimate of average nutrient intake by a group of healthy people that is assumed to be adequate. [cite: 9, 10, 11]

column1: The {{c1::Estimated Energy Requirement (EER)}} is the average dietary energy intake predicted to maintain {{c2::energy balance}} in a healthy adult. [cite: 12, 13]
column2: Unlike other nutrients, the EER is not set at a high percentile to avoid encouraging overconsumption and obesity. [cite: 12, 13]

column1: The {{c1::Upper Level of Intake (UL)}} is the highest average daily nutrient intake level likely to pose {{c2::no adverse effects}} to almost all individuals. [cite: 14, 15]
column2: As intake increases above the UL, the potential risk of adverse effects (toxicity) increases. [cite: 14, 15]

column1: The {{c1::Suggested Dietary Target (SDT)}} refers to a nutrient level that is specifically aimed at the {{c2::prevention of chronic disease}}. [cite: 16, 17]
column2: This is often used for nutrients like sodium or certain vitamins where higher or lower levels than the RDI may reduce disease risk. [cite: 16, 17]

column1: A nutrient intake level falling between the {{c1::EAR}} and the {{c2::RDI}} is categorized as {{c3::possibly inadequate}}. [cite: 18]
column2: While the individual might be meeting their needs, there is a risk they fall into the lower 50% of the population's requirement range. [cite: 18]

column1: An intake level between the {{c1::RDI}} and the {{c2::UL::Upper Level}} is considered {{c3::adequate}}. [cite: 19]
column2: This is the 'safe zone' where the requirement is almost certainly met without risk of toxicity. [cite: 19]

column1: Dietary fibre is frequently found on the {{c1::outer layer}} of grains and vegetables. [cite: 20]
column2: Refining grains often removes this outer layer (bran), significantly reducing the fibre content. [cite: 20]

column1: {{c1::Macronutrient distribution}} refers to the proportion of total {{c2::energy}} derived from each type of macronutrient (carbs, fats, proteins). [cite: 21]
column2: This is often expressed as a percentage of total kilojoules. [cite: 21]

column1: While the Mediterranean diet is considered balanced, the {{c1::Ornish::Diet name}} diet is characterized by being {{c2::low fat}} and high carbohydrate. [cite: 22, 23]
column2: The Ornish diet is often studied for its effects on heart disease reversal. [cite: 23]

column1: The {{c1::Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Range (AMDR)}} is a set of recommendations designed to ensure {{c2::adequate levels}} of each nutrient while reducing chronic disease risk. [cite: 24]
column2: It provides a range (e.g., 45-65% for carbs) rather than a single fixed number. [cite: 24]

column1: The four primary causes of nutrient deficiency include inadequate intake, inadequate {{c1::absorption}}, defective {{c2::utilisation}}, or increased {{c3::loss}} via urine or sweat. [cite: 25-29]
column2: Deficiencies can be primary (dietary) or secondary (physiological/pathological). [cite: 25-29]

column1: {{c1::Haem::Iron type}} iron is found in meat and is much {{c2::easier}} for the body to absorb than non-haem iron. [cite: 31, 32]
column2: Haem iron bypasses many of the absorption inhibitors that affect plant-based iron. [cite: 32]

column1: {{c1::Non-haem}} iron is found in foods like {{c2::grains, bread, and cereal}}. [cite: 33]
column2: Absorption of non-haem iron can be improved by consuming Vitamin C at the same meal. [cite: 33]

column1: Iron is a critical component of {{c1::haemoglobin}} and is also necessary for {{c2::energy generation}} and the {{c3::immune system}}. [cite: 34-36]
column2: Haemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. [cite: 34-36]

column1: The hormone responsible for the extraction and regulation of iron is {{c1::hepcidin}}. [cite: 37]
column2: Hepcidin controls iron flow into the plasma from macrophages, hepatocytes, and enterocytes. [cite: 37]

column1: In the iron cycle, the {{c1::liver}} and {{c2::spleen}} dismantle old red blood cells and package the reclaimed iron into {{c3::transferrin}}. [cite: 38, 39]
column2: This recycling process is vital as very little iron is excreted from the body naturally. [cite: 38, 39]

column1: {{c1::Transferrin}} is the protein that carries iron through the blood to the {{c2::muscles}} and {{c3::bone marrow}}. [cite: 40]
column2: High transferrin saturation can indicate iron overload, while low levels suggest deficiency. [cite: 40]

column1: The bone marrow uses iron to produce {{c1::haemoglobin}}, and any excess iron is stored in the protein {{c2::ferritin}}. [cite: 41]
column2: Ferritin levels in the blood are the most common way to assess a person's iron stores. [cite: 41]

column1: Calcium serves as the primary mineral for {{c1::bones}} and is also essential for the {{c2::nervous system}}. [cite: 42-45]
column2: In the nervous system, calcium is required for neurotransmitter release. [cite: 45]

column1: Calcium levels are regulated through three main mechanisms: GI absorption, renal excretion, and {{c1::bone mineralisation/demineralisation}}. [cite: 46-49]
column2: The body prioritizes blood calcium levels over bone density to maintain vital functions. [cite: 49]

column1: The absorption of calcium in the gastrointestinal tract is enhanced by {{c1::Vitamin D}}. [cite: 47]
column2: Without sufficient Vitamin D, only about 10-15% of dietary calcium is absorbed. [cite: 47]

column1: High levels of calcium can {{c1::interfere with}} the absorption of other micronutrients. [cite: 50]
column2: This is why calcium supplements are often taken away from other mineral-heavy meals. [cite: 50]

column1: When blood calcium is low, the {{c1::parathyroid hormone (PTH)}} and Vitamin D stimulate the {{c2::kidneys}} to reabsorb calcium. [cite: 51-53]
column2: This prevents the loss of calcium through urine. [cite: 53]

column1: A physiological response to low blood calcium is the {{c1::release}} of calcium from the {{c2::bones}}. [cite: 54]
column2: Chronic calcium deficiency leads to bone thinning (osteoporosis) because the body constantly 'borrows' calcium from the skeleton. [cite: 54]

column1: During Vitamin D synthesis in the skin, UV light converts {{c1::7-dehydrocholesterol}} to {{c2::previtamin D3}}. [cite: 58, 59]
column2: This is the first step of endogenous Vitamin D production. [cite: 59]

column1: {{c1::Body heat}} is required to convert previtamin D3 into its final form of {{c2::Vitamin D3}}. [cite: 60]
column2: This process does not require further UV exposure once the precursor is formed. [cite: 60]

column1: Vitamin D is a {{c1::fat-soluble}} vitamin; {{c2::Vitamin D2}} is found in plants, while {{c3::Vitamin D3}} is found in animals. [cite: 61-63]
column2: D3 is generally considered more effective at raising blood Vitamin D levels than D2. [cite: 61-63]

column1: The primary role of Vitamin D is to regulate the absorption of {{c1::calcium}} and {{c2::phosphorus}}. [cite: 65]
column2: These two minerals are the primary components of hydroxyapatite, the crystal that hardens bone. [cite: 65]

column1: Activation of Vitamin D involves the conversion of {{c1::25-hydroxyvitamin D}} (calcidiol) to {{c2::calcitriol}}. [cite: 67]
column2: Calcitriol is the biologically active form of the vitamin. [cite: 67]

column1: Vitamin B12 is frequently deficient in {{c1::vegan}} diets because it is primarily found in animal products. [cite: 68, 69]
column2: Vegans often require fortified foods or supplements to meet their B12 needs. [cite: 68, 69]

column1: Vitamin B12 interacts with {{c1::folate}} to facilitate the synthesis of {{c2::DNA}} and red blood cells (RBC). [cite: 70, 71]
column2: A deficiency in either can lead to megaloblastic anemia. [cite: 71]

column1: To absorb Vitamin B12 from the gut, the body requires {{c1::intrinsic factor}}, which is produced in the {{c2::stomach}}. [cite: 72, 73]
column2: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune condition where the body cannot produce intrinsic factor. [cite: 72, 73]

column1: Because Vitamin B12 is stored in the {{c1::liver}}, it can take {{c2::a few years}} for a deficiency to become symptomatic. [cite: 74, 75]
column2: This is unusual for water-soluble vitamins, which are typically not stored in large amounts. [cite: 74, 75]

column1: Physical symptoms of Vitamin B12 deficiency include fatigue, {{c1::large RBCs::blood cell trait}}, and {{c2::degenerative peripheral nerves}}. [cite: 76-79]
column2: Neurological damage from B12 deficiency can become permanent if not treated early. [cite: 78, 79]

column1: When diagnosing Vitamin B12 deficiency, it is vital to differentiate it from {{c1::folate deficiency}}. [cite: 80, 81]
column2: Giving folate to a B12-deficient person can mask the anemia while neurological damage continues. [cite: 81]

column1: Clinicians diagnose B12 deficiency by checking {{c1::serum B12}} levels followed by {{c2::biologically available}} B12. [cite: 82]
column2: Not all B12 in the blood is in a form the body can use. [cite: 82]

column1: A deficiency in Vitamin A is a major cause of {{c1::night blindness}}. [cite: 84]
column2: Vitamin A is essential for the health of the retina and the production of rhodopsin. [cite: 84]

column1: In Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, {{c1::pyruvate}} cannot be converted to {{c2::acetyl-CoA}}, resulting in less ATP production. [cite: 85]
column2: This affects the entry of carbohydrates into the Krebs cycle. [cite: 85]

column1: Increased {{c1::lactate}} levels in B1 deficiency cause {{c2::vasodilation}}, which leads to the development of {{c3::edema::swelling}}. [cite: 86]
column2: This is a hallmark of 'wet beriberi'. [cite: 86]

column1: Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency causes disruption in {{c1::glycolysis}} and the {{c2::Krebs cycle}}. [cite: 87, 88]
column2: B3 is a precursor to NAD and NADP, which are essential electron carriers. [cite: 88]

column1: B3 deficiency is rare but is historically associated with diets primarily consisting of {{c1::corn}}. [cite: 89]
column2: Corn is low in tryptophan, a precursor the body uses to synthesize its own niacin. [cite: 89]

column1: Scurvy is caused by a Vitamin C deficiency, which results in a lack of {{c1::collagen}} production. [cite: 90-92]
column2: Collagen is the main structural protein in connective tissues, leading to bleeding gums and poor wound healing in scurvy. [cite: 92]

column1: An iodine deficiency typically manifests as an {{c1::enlarged thyroid gland}} (goitre). [cite: 93, 94]
column2: The thyroid enlarges in an attempt to capture more iodine from the blood to produce hormones. [cite: 94]"

column1: Nutritional assessment & dietary guidelines,"6.6 Nutritional assessment & dietary guidelines - Clinical Practice
Comprehensive Assessment (ABCD)
•	Anthropometry: Weight, height, BMI ($kg/m^2$), waist circumference (risk: >94cm men, >80cm women). Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) for muscle wasting.
•	Biochemistry: Serum albumin (marker of inflammation/severity, not just nutrition), electrolytes, full blood count, and specific micronutrient assays.
•	Clinical: Physical exam for subcutaneous fat loss (temples, ribs), muscle wasting (quadriceps, deltoids), and fluid accumulation (edema/ascites).
•	Dietary: 24-hour recall, Food Frequency Questionnaires (FFQ), and weighted food records (gold standard but high burden).
Malnutrition Screening
•	Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST): Used to identify adults at risk based on BMI, unexplained weight loss, and acute disease effect.

•	Subjective Global Assessment (SGA): A clinical tool that correlates physical findings with medical history to grade malnutrition (A: Nourished, B: Mild/Moderate, C: Severe).","Approximately {{c1::20-50%}} of hospitalised patients are malnourished.
column2: This range reflects high prevalence across various clinical settings. [cite: 1]

column1: There are roughly {{c1::5400}} hospital-acquired cases of malnutrition annually.
column2: Hospital-acquired malnutrition occurs when a patient's status declines during their stay. [cite: 1]

column1: Malnutrition affects {{c1::32-72%}} of people in aged care.
column2: This indicates that older adults in care are at particularly high risk. [cite: 1]

column1: Roughly {{c1::30%}} of the general population has some form of malnutrition.
column2: Malnutrition can encompass both undernutrition and poor nutrient quality. [cite: 1]

column1: Malnutrition leads to significant issues with {{c1::wound healing}} and recovery from illness.
column2: Adequate protein and micronutrients are essential for tissue repair. [cite: 1]

column1: Malnourished patients experience increased {{c1::infections}} and {{c2::complications}} during recovery.
column2: Malnutrition severely compromises the immune system. [cite: 1]

column1: In the ABCD assessment framework, **A** stands for {{c1::Anthropometry}}.
column2: This involves physical measurements of the human body. [cite: 1]

column1: Examples of **Anthropometry** (the 'A' in ABCD) include {{c1::height}}, {{c2::weight}}, and {{c3::BMI}}.
column2: These are fundamental baseline measurements. [cite: 1]

column1: In the ABCD assessment framework, **B** stands for {{c1::Biochemistry}}.
column2: This refers to laboratory data and blood markers. [cite: 1]

column1: Biochemical blood levels are often {{c1::not helpful::helpful/not helpful}} for diagnosing malnutrition.
column2: Systemic inflammation and hydration status can easily skew these values. [cite: 1]

column1: When performing nutritional Biochemistry (the 'B' in ABCD), practitioners should **not** use {{c1::albumin}} or {{c2::prealbumin}}.
column2: These are negative acute-phase reactants that drop during stress/inflammation, making them unreliable markers of nutrition. [cite: 1]

column1: In the ABCD assessment framework, **C** stands for {{c1::Clinical}}.
column2: This involves a physical examination for signs of deficiency, such as muscle wasting. [cite: 1]

column1: In the ABCD assessment framework, **D** stands for {{c1::Dietary}}.
column2: This involves evaluating a patient's food and nutrient intake. [cite: 1]

column1: The acronym **MUST** stands for the {{c1::Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool}}.
column2: It is used to systematically identify individuals at risk. [cite: 1]

column1: The primary purpose of the MUST tool is to determine {{c1::who is at risk of malnutrition}}.
column2: It is a screening tool, not a full diagnostic assessment. [cite: 1]

column1: Performing a MUST screening requires two specific pieces of data: {{c1::BMI}} and {{c2::weight history}}.
column2: Weight history is essential for identifying unintentional weight loss. [cite: 1]

column1: A {{c1::DEXA scan}} is a measurement method that is {{c2::expensive}} and involves exposure to {{c3::radiation}}.
column2: While accurate for body composition, these factors limit its routine use. [cite: 1]

column1: For men, the target **waist circumference** to minimize health risk is less than {{c1::94}} cm.
column2: Measurements above this are linked to metabolic complications. [cite: 1]

column1: For women, the target **waist circumference** to minimize health risk is less than {{c1::80}} cm.
column2: This threshold helps screen for abdominal obesity. [cite: 1]

column1: The target **Waist:Height ratio** for optimal health is below {{c1::0.5}}.
column2: This ratio is often considered a better health indicator than BMI for diverse body types. [cite: 1]

column1: **Dietary recall** methods, such as the 24-hour recall, are categorized as {{c1::retrospective}}.
column2: They rely on the participant's memory of past consumption. [cite: 1]

column1: A **24-hour recall** is a {{c1::retrospective}} method of dietary assessment.
column2: It is quick but may not represent usual long-term intake. [cite: 1]

column1: A **Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ)** is a retrospective tool typically used for {{c1::large populations}}.
column2: It is efficient for identifying broad dietary patterns over time. [cite: 1]

column1: A **dietary record** (logging food as it is eaten) is a {{c1::prospective}} assessment method.
column2: Prospective methods record intake in real-time. [cite: 1]

column1: A **dietary record** involves the process of {{c1::logging food}}.
column2: This reduces memory bias but may influence the user to eat 'better' while recording. [cite: 1]

column1: **Nutrient Reference Values (NRV)** provide the fundamental data used for {{c1::Core food group analysis}}.
column2: These values define the requirements for various nutrients. [cite: 1]

column1: The two primary Australian dietary guideline documents are the {{c1::Australian Dietary Guidelines}} and the {{c2::Australian Guide to Healthy Eating}}.
column2: These provide the framework for public health nutrition. [cite: 1]

column1: Guideline 1: Be {{c1::physically active}} and consume nutrient levels to meet {{c2::energy}} needs.
column2: This focuses on maintaining energy balance. [cite: 1]

column1: Guideline 2: Enjoy a wide variety of foods from the {{c1::five}} food groups.
column2: Variety is essential to ensure all micronutrient needs are met. [cite: 1]

column1: Guideline 3: Limit intake of {{c1::saturated fat}}, {{c2::added salt}}, {{c3::added sugars}}, and {{c4::alcohol}}.
column2: These items are risk factors for chronic diseases. [cite: 1]

column1: Guideline 4: Encourage, support, and promote {{c1::breastfeeding}}.
column2: This guideline is specifically aimed at infant health and maternal support. [cite: 1]

column1: Guideline 5: Care for your food; prepare and store it safely to ensure it is not {{c1::contaminated}}.
column2: This focuses on food safety and prevention of foodborne illness. [cite: 1]

column1: Only {{c1::2%}} of Australians follow the recommended dietary guidelines.
column2: This statistic highlights a significant public health challenge in dietary adherence. [cite: 1]"

column1: Altered nutrition requirements, myths & misconceptions,"6.7 Altered nutrition requirements, myths & misconceptions - Extended Study
Life Stage Transitions

•	Pregnancy: Increased need for folate (prevent neural tube defects), Iron (blood volume expansion), and Iodine (fetal brain development). Energy needs only increase significantly in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters.
•	Infancy: Exclusive breastfeeding recommended for the first 6 months. High energy requirements per kg of body weight due to rapid growth.
•	Older Adults: Sarcopenia (muscle loss) increases protein requirements. Vitamin B12 absorption often decreases due to atrophic gastritis.
Refeeding Syndrome Pathophysiology
•	Mechanism: Chronic malnutrition leads to intracellular electrolyte depletion. Reintroduction of carbohydrates causes an insulin spike, driving phosphate, magnesium, and potassium into cells.
•	Consequences: Severe hypophosphatemia, cardiac arrhythmias, respiratory failure, and sudden death.
•	Prevention Protocol: Identify high-risk patients (BMI <16, 15% weight loss in 3-6 months). Start calories slowly (e.g., 10 kcal/kg/day). Mandatory Thiamin (100mg) before feeding.
Nutrition Myths vs. Science
•	Food-based vs. Nutrient-based: Single nutrient focus (e.g., 'fat is bad') often fails compared to whole dietary patterns (e.g., Mediterranean diet).

•	Supplementation: For healthy individuals with balanced diets, supplements often provide no additional benefit and may reach 'Upper Level' (UL) toxicity in some cases.","Individual {{c1::health literacy}} is defined as the ability to make good decisions about health and take appropriate action
